{{short description|Geometric solid between two parallel surfaces}}
[[File:Prism, frustum, prismatoid and scutoid.svg|thumb|alt=Alt text|A scutoid compared with a [[Prism (geometry)|prism]], [[frustum]], and [[prismatoid]]]]
[[File:Scutoids.gif|thumb|Two 5-6 scutoids, flipped and attached]]
A '''scutoid''' is a particular type of [[geometric solid]] between two parallel surfaces. The boundary of each of the surfaces (and of all the other parallel surfaces between them) either is a [[polygon]] or resembles a polygon, but is not necessarily planar, and the [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of the two end polygons are joined by either a curve or a Y-shaped connection on at least one of the edges, but not necessarily all of the edges. Scutoids present at least one [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] between these two planes. Scutoids are not necessarily convex, and lateral faces are not necessarily planar, so several scutoids can  pack together to fill all the space between the two parallel surfaces. They may be more generally described as a mix between a [[frustum]] and a [[prismatoid]].<ref name="natcomm2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez-Gálvez |first1=Pedro |last2=Vicente-Munuera |first2=Pablo |last3=Tagua |first3=Antonio |last4=Forja |first4=Cristina |last5=Castro |first5=Ana M. |last6=Letrán |first6=Marta |last7=Valencia-Expósito |first7=Andrea |last8=Grima |first8=Clara|author8-link=Clara Grima |last9=Bermúdez-Gallardo |first9=Marina |date=2018-07-27 |title= Scutoids are a geometrical solution to three-dimensional packing of epithelia |journal= Nature Communications |language= en |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=2960 |doi=10.1038/s41467-018-05376-1  |doi-access=free|pmid=30054479 |issn=2041-1723|pmc=6063940 |bibcode=2018NatCo...9.2960G }}</ref><ref name="burdick">{{Cite magazine |last= Burdick |first= Alan |date= 30 July 2018 |title= We Are All Scutoids: A Brand-New Shape, Explained |magazine= The New Yorker |language= en-US |url= https://www.newyorker.com/elements/lab-notes/we-are-all-scutoids-a-brand-new-shape-explained |access-date= 2024-11-27 }}</ref>

==Naming==
The object was first described by Gómez-Gálvez ''et al.'' in a paper entitled ''Scutoids are a geometrical solution to three-dimensional packing of epithelia'', and published in July 2018.<ref name="natcomm2018"/> Officially, the name ''scutoid'' was coined because of its resemblance to the shape of the [[Notum|scutum]] and [[Scutellum (insect anatomy)|scutellum]] in some insects, such as beetles in the subfamily [[Cetoniinae]].<ref name="natcomm2018"/> Unofficially, [[Clara Grima]] has stated that while working on the project, the shape was temporarily called an ''Escu''-toid as a joke after the biology group leader [[Luis M. Escudero]].{{sfn|Parker|2018}}<ref>{{cite web |title= Supplementary Movie |website= static-content.springer.com |type= |series= from {{harvnb|Gómez-Gálvez|Vicente-Munuera|Tagua|Forja|2018|loc=Electronic supplementary material}} |url= https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-018-05376-1/MediaObjects/41467_2018_5376_MOESM3_ESM.avi |access-date= Nov 27, 2024 }}</ref> Since his last name, "[[:wikt:escudero|Escudero]]", means "squire" (from Latin ''scutarius'' = shield-bearer), the temporary name was modified slightly to become "scutoid".

== Appearance in nature ==
{{Quote box
| align = right
| width = 30%
| quote = "The shape, however odd, is a building block of multicellular organisms; complex life might never have emerged on Earth without it."
|author = Alan Burdick
|source = ''We Are All Scutoids: A Brand New Shape, Explained''<ref name="burdick"/>
}}

[[Epithelium|Epithelial]] cells adopt the "scutoidal shape" under certain circumstances.<ref name="natcomm2018"/> In epithelia, cells can 3D-pack as scutoids, facilitating tissue curvature. This is fundamental to the shaping of the organs during development.<ref name="natcomm2018"/><ref>{{Cite news |last= Boddy |first= Jessica |date= 2018-07-27 |title= The 'Scutoid' Is Geometry's Newest Shape, and It Could Be All Over Your Body |work= Gizmodo |language= en-US |url= https://gizmodo.com/the-scutoid-is-geometrys-newest-shape-and-it-could-be-1827924643 |access-date= 2024-11-27 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last= Georgiou |first= Aristos |title= Scientists have discovered a brand-new three-dimensional shape|date=2018-07-27 |work= Newsweek |language= en |url= https://www.newsweek.com/scutoid-scientists-discover-entirely-new-shape-and-its-been-hiding-inside-1045097 |access-date= 2024-11-27 }}</ref>

<blockquote>"Scutoid is a [[prismatoid]] to which one extra mid-level [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]] has been added. This extra vertex forces some of the "[[Face (geometry)|faces]]" of the resulting object to curve. This means that Scutoids are not [[polyhedra]], because not all of their faces are [[Plane (geometry)|planar]]. ... For the computational biologists who created/discovered the Scutoid, the key property of the shape is that it can combine with itself and other geometric objects like frustums to create 3D packings of epithelial cells."<br /> - [[Laura Taalman]]<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=1023371252663312385 |first= Laura |last= Taalman |author-link= Laura Taalman |user= mathgrrl |title= Have you read the @Nature article introducing the new mathematical shape called the SCUTOID? This cutting-edge science is now 3D printable: https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:3024272 |date= 28 July 2018 |access-date= Nov 27, 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= Taalman |first= Laura |author-link= Laura Taalman |date= July 29, 2018 |title= Pair of Packable Scutoids |website= mathgrrl.com |url= https://mathgrrl.com/hacktastic/2018/07/pairs-of-packable-scutoids/ |access-date= 2024-11-27 }}</ref></blockquote>

Cells in the developing lung epithelium have been found to have more complex shapes than the term "scutoid", inspired by the simple scutellum of beetles, suggests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez |first1=Harold F. |last2=Dumond |first2=Mathilde |last3=Hodel |first3=Leonie |last4=Vetter |first4=Roman |last5=Iber |first5=Dagmar |date=2021-10-05 |title=3D cell neighbour dynamics in growing pseudostratified epithelia |journal=eLife |language=En |volume=10 |article-number=e68135 |doi=10.7554/eLife.68135 |pmid=34609280 |pmc=8570695 |doi-access=free }}</ref> When "scutoids" exhibit multiple Y-shaped connections or vertices along their axis, they have therefore been called "punakoids" instead,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Iber |first1=Dagmar |last2=Vetter |first2=Roman |date=2022-05-12 |title=3D Organisation of Cells in Pseudostratified Epithelia |journal=Frontiers in Physics |language=En |volume=10 |article-number=898160 |doi=10.3389/fphy.2022.898160 |bibcode=2022FrP....10.8160I |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/547113 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> as their shape is more reminiscent of the [[Pancake Rocks]] in [[Punakaiki]], [[New Zealand]].

== Potential uses==
The scutoid explains how [[epithelial cells]] (the cells that line and protect organs such as the skin) efficiently pack in three dimensions.<ref name="natcomm2018"/> As epithelial tissue bends or grows, the cells have to take on new shapes to pack together using the least amount of energy possible, and until the scutoid's discovery, it was assumed that epithelial cells packed in mostly frustums, as well as other [[prism (geometry)|prism]]-like shapes. Now, with the knowledge of how epithelial cells pack, it opens up many new possibilities in terms of [[artificial organ]]s. The scutoid may be applied to making better artificial organs, allowing for things like effective organ replacements, recognizing whether a person's cells are packing correctly or not, and ways to fix that problem.{{sfn|Parker|2018}}
